input.question: If an object (such as a lightbulb) falls and shatters, can its much tinier components (such as microscopic shards) bounce up higher than the object's original drop height?
input.ground_truth: It is not impossible for this to happen in general. The relevant concept is momentum (p=mv). For situations like this it is often helpful to think of an extreme situation. Imagine dropping an anvil with a whoopee cushion taped to the bottom and a ping-pong ball in the hole of the whoopee cushion. So it will depend on the nature of the object, which in this case is a light bulb. I would think experimental data would be in needed unfortunately.

Okay! Imagine you have a big glass lightbulb. You drop it on the floor, and it breaks into lots of tiny, tiny pieces called shards.

Now, when the lightbulb falls, it goes down and then hits the floor. When it breaks, those little shards fly everywhere.

Sometimes, a tiny shard might hit the floor and bounce up really high! Even higher than the lightbulb went up before you dropped it.

How is that possible? Well, when the lightbulb breaks, the energy that was in the whole bulb can go into each little piece. If one tiny shard gets a lot of that energy, it can zoom up higher than the whole bulb did.

But most of the time, the little pieces don’t go as high as the big bulb did. It’s like if you have a big cookie and you break it into crumbs—sometimes a crumb might fly farther than the whole cookie, but usually, the big cookie goes farther.

So yes, sometimes the tiny shards can bounce higher than the lightbulb did! But it’s not always true for every piece.
